Daniel’s “context” framing is productive, but it quietly smuggles in a strong assumption: that careless mistakes mostly indicate an *incomplete* context. Often they do—but plenty of errors come from the *wrong* context (a bad model that feels complete), from cue-dependent retrieval (the right knowledge not activating under exam-like conditions), or from attention and working-memory limits that have little to do with what one “forgot to load.” Cognitive Load Theory explicitly separates the *structure* of knowledge from the *capacity* to deploy it under pressure; the same learner can “have” the context and still drop steps when the task overwhelms working memory ([Sweller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_load_theory)). If Daniel means “context” to include attention-management and chunking, that should be stated, because otherwise the claim risks blaming the learner’s model for what is sometimes a bottleneck in execution.

A helpful expansion is to distinguish between “loading context” as *review* versus as *retrieval practice*. Recaps can become comforting re-reading, which feels like loading but doesn’t reliably train the ability to reconstruct the model from sparse cues. What Daniel calls “practice loading the context” aligns closely with the testing effect: repeatedly *rebuilding* the context from memory in varied situations, not just re-exposing oneself to it ([Roediger & Karpicke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Testing_effect)). That also connects to schema theories of learning—knowledge as organized structures that guide perception and action ([schema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schema_(psychology))): mastery is less “complete context” than “fast, correct schema selection under the right triggers.” Naming that distinction would sharpen the post: the real skill is not only acquiring a model, but making it reliably *callable* and *switchable* across contexts.
